headline: Bond yields climbed around the world on Monday, pushing the 10-year Treasury back to 5.15% a week before the Fed meets.
dateline: Tuesday, October 20, 2026 · closes as of Mon Oct 19

rundown.h: Markets see a pause next week, then a December hike.
rundown.p: CME FedWatch pricing put the odds of a hold on Oct 28 at about 85% as of Oct 16, while the odds of a December hike stood near 93.5% on Oct 20. For borrowers, a pause buys weeks, not relief.

rundown.h: Shoppers spent more in September, mostly at the pump.
rundown.p: Retail sales rose 0.8% in September, well above the 0.3% forecast, and August was revised up to 1.3%. But gas station sales jumped 6.4%, sales excluding gasoline rose just 0.2%, and the control group that feeds GDP edged up only 0.1%. Fuel is crowding out other spending, a soft spot for retail tenants.

rundown.h: Bank stocks keep sliding even as credit stays clean.
rundown.p: The KBW Nasdaq Bank Index has fallen six straight weeks, down 11% since early September, the longest losing streak for big-bank stocks since summer 2008. Results tell a calmer story: Fifth Third's net charge-offs were 0.31% of loans, and Zions' fell to $3 million from $56 million a year earlier. Investors seem to be pricing the rate outlook, not loan losses.
rundown.src: Yahoo Finance; Fifth Third, Zions releases · Oct 19

rundown.h: KeyCorp beat on profit, with record revenue.
rundown.p: KeyCorp earned $0.51 a share in the third quarter, up 24% from a year ago and ahead of the roughly $0.46 expected, on record revenue of $2.04 billion, a hair below the $2.05 billion consensus. Net interest margin was 2.95%, and Key bought back $320 million of stock. Shares edged up before the open.
rundown.src: KeyCorp via PR Newswire; Investing.com · Oct 20

rundown.h: Netflix reports tonight; Tesla follows on Wednesday.
rundown.p: Netflix reports after today's close, with analysts looking for about $0.82 a share and a read on ad revenue and free cash flow. Tesla reports Oct 21, not today, after third-quarter deliveries of 486,532 beat forecasts by about 5%; its capital spending is estimated near $7.5 billion, versus $2.3 billion a year earlier.

dive.title: Warehouses are filling faster than builders can add them
dive.dek: After two years of oversupply, U.S. industrial demand has beaten new construction for two straight quarters, and developers are breaking ground again.
dive.body:
The warehouse glut is clearing. Cushman & Wakefield's third-quarter report, out Oct 12, puts national industrial vacancy at 6.8%, 20bp below its late-2025 peak and the lowest since the end of 2024. Tenants absorbed a net 76.6 million sq ft in the quarter, the most since early 2023, while about 64 million sq ft was completed. New leasing topped 200 million sq ft for a second straight quarter, and big-box space of 500,000 sq ft or more saw vacancy drop 280bp from a year earlier to 7.4%.

The biggest landlord says the same. Prologis reported period-end occupancy of 95.6% on Oct 15, signed about 60 million sq ft of leases, and narrowed its 2026 core FFO guidance to $6.25–$6.29 a share. Its CEO said customers are running lean on inventory and that excess space in their networks has largely been absorbed. Rents on new leases there came in 38% above the expiring ones on a net effective basis.

The catch is that the easy rent gains are fading and supply is coming back. Yardi Matrix data through August show in-place rents up 5.4% from a year ago, but the gap between new-lease and in-place rents has shrunk to $0.88 a sq ft, from $2.45 two years ago. Cushman counts about 324 million sq ft under construction, up 23% from a year earlier and the most since mid-2024, and Yardi's tally of 2026 starts is the highest since 2022. Import volumes add another question: the NRF expects October imports up 8.5% from a year ago, then a 1% decline in November as the stretched-out peak season ends.

For owners and lenders, a tighter market supports values and refinancing even with a 10-year above 5%. Firms measure vacancy differently, so the direction matters more than the level. What would change the picture: a 2027 wave of completions from today's starts, a slowdown in imports and consumer spending, or the other big brokers' third-quarter numbers failing to confirm the decline.

table.cap: Industrial real estate, by the numbers
rows: Yardi Matrix via CRE Daily, Oct 1

items.title: September PPI: producer prices jumped 1.3%, the annual rate hit 6.3%

chart.t: PPI final demand, % change from a year earlier
chart.src: Source: BLS via FRED (series PPIFIS, index levels; year-over-year changes computed).

items.body:
Producer prices for final demand rose 1.3% in September, against a 0.5% consensus and 0.5% in August, the biggest monthly gain since 2022. The annual rate climbed to 6.3% from 5.6%, its highest since December 2022. Excluding food and energy, prices rose 0.7% for the month and 5.0% from a year earlier, up from 3.0% in September 2025.

Goods prices rose 2.6% in the month, the most since the series began in 2009, led by energy (+10.8%) and gasoline (+20.3%). Services rose 0.8%, with wholesale margins for machinery and vehicles up 3.9%. Further up the pipeline, processed intermediate goods were 14.1% higher than a year earlier and unprocessed goods 21.5% higher.

Bonds rallied anyway on release day: the 2-year yield fell 5bp to 4.77% and the 10-year 9bp to 5.10%, a move Sigro Research tied mostly to a falling term premium.

experts.who: Brian Wesbury and Robert Stein, First Trust
experts.view: Said energy explained more than 40% of the jump, but prices outside energy also rose 0.7%, a sign that fuel costs are spreading through the economy.
Argued the report backs up September's CPI in showing inflation moving the wrong way for the Fed.

items.lean: The economists quoted read the print as inflation broadening; rate markets largely looked through it on the day.
items.src: Sources: Trading Economics (PPI release, Oct 15); First Trust (components, Oct 15); FRED PPIFIS (Oct 15); Sigro Research (yields, Oct 16); Axios (Oct 15).

lead.title: Iran widens its threats from tankers to undersea cables
lead.body:
Iran raised the stakes beyond shipping over the weekend. On Oct 18 security chief Mohsen Rezaei warned that data centers, undersea cables and AI facilities could be targets if the U.S. and Israel resume strikes, and on Oct 19 a Revolutionary Guards spokesman pointed to seven major cables running under the strait. The Guards also said another tanker caught fire after hitting a mine, and Iran's new strait authority has put 122 ships on a blacklist. U.S. Central Command said a container ship, the GFS Pride, sank under tow after being hit by an Iranian projectile.

Diplomacy is busier but has produced nothing concrete. Russia's Lavrov met Iran's president and foreign minister in Tehran on Oct 19, and Pakistan's army chief, Gen. Asim Munir, travels there today as a U.S.–Iran go-between. Qatar says talks are ongoing.
lead.reach: Still mainly through oil and fuel. Energy Secretary Wright said Gulf oil flows are back to about 80% of pre-war levels (Oct 19), but refined products remain tight; dated Brent, the physical benchmark, was near $117, almost $16 below a week earlier (Bloomberg via Rigzone, Oct 19).

views.view: See the market pricing in a substantial risk premium because the situation is so volatile.

views.who: June Goh, senior oil analyst, Sparta Commodities
views.view: Thinks a weak global economy limits how much higher prices can go, and expects Brent to stay roughly range-bound around $100.

hot.chg: Oct 19: IRGC flags seven undersea cables as possible targets; 122 ships blacklisted; another tanker reported mined.

reading.title: A Dollar a Share, and a World at War
reading.dek: In 1939, as Europe went to war, a 26-year-old Templeton borrowed $10,000 and bought shares in every NYSE company trading for a dollar or less.
reading.body:
In the late summer of 1939, as Germany's invasion of Poland plunged Europe into war, American investors had every reason to avoid stocks. A decade of depression had already flattened markets, and now a second global conflict loomed. A 26-year-old money manager from Tennessee named John Templeton read the same headlines and reached the opposite conclusion. He borrowed $10,000 and told his broker to buy 100 shares of every company on the New York Stock Exchange trading at a dollar or less.

The order swept up 104 companies, and many were in miserable shape: by most accounts, more than 30 were already in bankruptcy. Templeton was not betting that each business was sound. His bet was that the whole basket was priced for catastrophe. If war revived American industry, as he expected, demand for steel, railcars and manufactured goods would lift even the weakest names, and the stocks priced for failure had the most room to rebound. Where others saw only risk, he saw lopsided odds.

He was right. As wartime production ramped up, the portfolio rallied. Only four of the 104 holdings ended up worthless, and within a few years the stake had roughly quadrupled, to around $40,000, according to accounts of the trade. Sources differ on exactly when he sold, but the lesson was clear: buying broadly at the moment of deepest gloom had paid off handsomely.

The trade became the founding legend of a remarkable career. Templeton, a Yale graduate and Rhodes Scholar at Oxford's Balliol College, launched the Templeton Growth Fund in 1954 and became one of the first prominent American managers to hunt for bargains around the world rather than at home alone. He renounced his U.S. citizenship in 1964, later settled full-time in the Bahamas, and in 1992 sold his fund business to the Franklin group for $440 million. Knighted in 1987 for his philanthropy, he also created the Templeton Prize, and he died in Nassau in 2008 at 95.

His enduring idea, usually summarized as buying when pessimism peaks, was less about bravado than discipline. Templeton diversified widely, accepted that some bets would fail, and insisted on prices low enough that the survivors would more than cover the losers. The 1939 order captured all three principles at once: breadth, humility and price. It remains a template investors revisit whenever fear, rather than fundamentals, seems to be setting prices. The hard part, then as now, is acting while the news is still getting worse instead of waiting for an all-clear.
takeaways: War headlines are setting oil prices again; Templeton asked what fear had already priced in.
After the AI selloff, his lesson is breadth: many cheap bets, not one hero pick.
A 5%-plus 10-year raises the bar: a bargain has to beat a safe yield.
